title: Helping Students Understand Motivation
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart answers the question left open in his previous post: what tools help students motivate themselves? He argues that the real goal is helping students motivate themselves rather than motivating them, and he identifies character strengths as one promising track. Using Character Lab's list, he claims that four and a half of the strengths are motivational in nature: the passion half of grit, purpose, curiosity, gratitude and flexible (not blind) optimism. He explains how each fuels effort, for example how gratitude wards off motivation-depleting thought patterns. His main practical move is self-experimentation: teachers should first build these strengths in themselves, reflect on the process, and extrapolate strategies for students. He illustrates with his own effort to cultivate curiosity about ancient history and his distinction between painful curiosity that only wonders and productive curiosity that acts.
points: Stuart reframes the motivation problem from "How can I motivate my students?" to the harder and better goal of helping students motivate themselves.
He argues that roughly half the character strengths are motivational: grit's passion component, purpose, curiosity, gratitude and flexible optimism.
Gratitude motivates both by supplying reasons to work and by warding off depleting thoughts such as "I deserve better than this."
The most promising way to build these strengths in students is for teachers to self-experiment with them first and share what they learn.
His distinction between painful curiosity, which wonders without acting, and productive curiosity, which wonders and acts, gives students a usable tool.
quotes: And I've also taught long enough to know that simply being an inspirational teacher isn't enough; I'm not satisfied with giving them goosebumps in class. I want to give them knowledge about their aspirations, their current conditions, and how to do the work to connect those two things.

And I think that phrase is so, so important in this discussion: we're trying to help our students motivate themselves. That's an Everest worth climbing, much more so than “How can I motivate my students?

Passion is what I consider the motivational element — passion makes teachers stick to their work, and artists, and engineers, and parents, and priests, and social workers. Persistence, on the other hand, isn't motivation — it's motivation's product. Gritty people use passion to produce persistence toward long-term ends.

The habitually grateful is more motivated both because of the reasons they have to work hard and because of the effectiveness with which they ward off motivation-depleting thought patterns (“I'm grateful I get this opportunity” versus “I deserve better than this;” “I get to go to school today” versus “Why do I have to learn boring world history?”).

The most promising way, for several reasons, is to first build them in ourselves with an eye toward what's happening as we do so. In short: self-experimentation. Which is lots of fun because, as you go about self-experimenting with this stuff, you learn how to get better at life.

This has taught me (and I've shared the revelation with my students) that there are two kinds of curiosity: productive and painful. The painful kind wonders but does not act; the productive kind wonders and acts.

It's key to remind ourselves, again and again, that the character strengths are strengthenable — this is why we don't call them traits. They're not an eye color; they're a muscle. And the more we strengthen them in ourselves — and experience the fun, “Oh, ancient world history is actually kind of cool” breakthroughs — the more we're bound to strengthen them in our students.
